BABYBABY GUIDES / PLAY & DEVELOPMENT

Play without a toy haul.

Your face, a familiar song, a book, and a few carefully chosen objects can give you plenty to do together. Start with what your baby is interested in today.

By BabyBaby · November 26, 2026 · 5 min read

In this guide

Start with their interestChoose objects carefullyFour simple ways to playMake room for repetitionAdapt the invitationSources

It can be hard to know what to do with a baby between feeds, changes, and sleep. The NHS suggests books, songs, and things already around the home as ways to play. You can begin with a small moment together rather than a shopping list.

These ideas are invitations to try while your baby is awake and an adult is actively watching. Choose the version that suits what your child can comfortably do. Age ranges are rough starting points, not a timetable to meet.

Notice, join in, then leave a little space.

What has caught your baby's attention: your face, a sound, the page of a book? Join that interest. Say a few words, copy a sound, or show one simple action. Then pause so they have a chance to respond.

UNICEF describes play as a way for babies to explore, practise skills, and connect with caregivers. Its ideas include taking turns with sounds and copying a baby's actions. You can offer opportunities to look, listen, reach, or respond without expecting a particular result.

One invitation is enough. Put one suitable object in view, or begin one game. You can repeat it if your baby remains interested. If they turn away, become upset, or need a feed or rest, pause and respond to that need.

Everyday objects still need a safety check.

Something being in your kitchen does not make it suitable for a baby. Stay close and actively watch throughout. If you need to step away, stop the activity and put your baby in an appropriate safe place.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission advises following toy age labels, keeping small parts away from children under three, and removing plastic packaging. For objects at home, inspect the whole item and anything that could break or detach.

  • Choose clean, sturdy, unbreakable items with smooth edges and no loose parts. Check them again after play.
  • Leave out small lids, coins, beads, balloons, plastic bags, cords, and items with sharp edges. Supervision does not make a choking hazard suitable.
  • Keep remote controls, keys, and other adult gadgets out of the play selection. The NHS warns that button batteries can cause severe internal injury; keep them inaccessible.
  • For purchased toys, follow the manufacturer's safety instructions and age guidance. An older sibling's toy may have parts that are unsuitable for a baby.

If you are unsure whether an object is suitable, choose a familiar baby toy or a game that needs no object.

Four simple ways to play.

1. Your face and voice

For a young baby who is alert and comfortable: Hold them securely, with their head supported, and bring your face into view. Smile, make a gentle sound, and wait. Answer a sound or expression if one comes. There is no need to move their hands or get them to copy you.

This is a simple version of UNICEF's back-and-forth talking activity. A brief exchange can be the whole game.

2. One page, one sound

From early infancy, adapted as your baby grows: Share a sturdy baby book you already have or borrow one. Point to a picture, name it, or make an animal sound. If your baby is looking at another part of the page, follow that instead. You do not have to finish the book.

The NHS recommends looking at books from an early age and notes that libraries often have children's books. For a baby who can handle pages, let them explore while you help keep the book comfortable to hold.

3. A small puppet conversation

For a baby interested in watching your hand: Put a clean, plain sock over your own hand. Give it a voice, let it say hello, then wait. Keep it on your hand and in view; leave off buttons, glued-on eyes, ribbons, or other decorations. If your baby would rather watch your face, the puppet can retire.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) includes sock-puppet play among its simple activities for young babies. You can use your ordinary voice and a song your family already knows.

4. Tap, pause, and listen

For an older baby who sits steadily and handles objects: Sit with them on the floor, away from cooking. Offer a lightweight, unbreakable bowl and a short, smooth spoon that you have checked for damage and loose parts. Show one gentle tap, then pause. Your baby might tap, touch the bowl, or simply listen.

The AAP suggests simple homemade drums around 10–12 months. Keep the sound gentle, remove any damaged item, and end the activity if your baby is uncomfortable. Choose another game if the objects are not suitable for your child.

You can do the same thing again.

A familiar game does not need a new twist every time. You might offer the same book tomorrow, pause in the same song, or repeat the puppet's greeting. Notice what your baby does with the opportunity rather than trying to make each session more advanced.

Keep the invitation small enough to fit your day. There is no required number of games, no result to photograph, and no need to record every response. Sometimes the useful thing to notice is that your baby has had enough.

Change the activity to fit your child.

You can hold the book yourself, keep an object still for longer, make a sound softer, or play without asking your baby to reach. UNICEF encourages adapting its activities for children with different abilities. If your child has a care or therapy plan, follow the guidance from their team.

These games are not developmental tests. If you are worried about what your child can see, hear, or do, bring that question to their clinician. You do not need to keep repeating an activity to find the answer yourself.

For today, choose one invitation you can enjoy together. It can be as small as a song and a pause.
